title: Judicial Review

endcard.line: Pictures: MohitSingh (CC BY 3.0); unknown photographer (public domain)

segments.say: Suppose a law takes away one of your Fundamental Rights. Does it stand just because it was passed? In India, the courts can strike it down.

anim.title: Article 13
items: The State shall not make laws that take away Fundamental Rights
A law that does is void
Only to the extent it clashes

segments.say: Article thirteen says the State shall not make any law that takes away or abridges the Fundamental Rights. A law that does is void, to the extent it clashes.

Article thirty-two makes the right to approach the Supreme Court for these rights a Fundamental Right itself. Article two twenty-six lets High Courts issue writs for these rights and for any other purpose.
Both can issue five writs: habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari.
Review reached even amendments to the Constitution. In nineteen seventy-three, thirteen judges heard the Kesavananda Bharati case, the largest bench ever.
By seven to six, the court held that Parliament can amend the Constitution, but cannot destroy its basic structure.
For GS Two, link judicial review to Articles thirteen, thirty-two and two twenty-six, and to the basic structure doctrine.

sources: Constitution of India, official English text (Legislative Department diglot PDF, legislative.gov.in, 'as on' 2024 edition): Art. 13(1)–(2) (laws inconsistent with or in derogation of Fundamental Rights void to the extent of the inconsistency; State shall not make laws taking away or abridging them); Art. 32 (right to move the Supreme Court guaranteed; writs in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari); Art. 226 (High Courts' power to issue the same writs for the enforcement of Part III rights and for any other purpose)

Wikipedia, 'Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala' (read): 1973; heard by the largest-ever Constitution Bench of 13 judges; verdict divided 7–6; Parliament has wide amending powers but cannot destroy the basic structure

quiz.q: Which Article makes the right to move the Supreme Court a Fundamental Right?
How does a High Court's writ power differ from the Supreme Court's?
options: High Courts can also issue writs 'for any other purpose'
High Courts cannot issue habeas corpus
High Courts need the President's leave
quiz.why: Art. 226 adds 'and for any other purpose'.

quiz.q: In Kesavananda Bharati (1973), the court held that Parliament…
options: cannot amend Fundamental Rights at all
can amend any part without limit
must hold a referendum to amend
cannot destroy the Constitution's basic structure
